node.label: Philip J Deloria
node.date_label: Playing Indian (1998) · Indians in Unexpected Places (2004) · Becoming Mary Sully: Toward an American Indian Abstract (2019)
node.description: A historian of American Indian peoples, representation and modernity. His selected bibliography includes Playing Indian, Indians in Unexpected Places and the recovery of artist Mary Sully’s work. In the publisher’s 2024 written Q&A he rejects a categorical separation of Indigenous people from modernity while describing Sully’s distinctive artistic position. The same account explains how family preservation, research, public talks and curatorial questions helped turn overlooked drawings into a historical argument and exhibitions; that collaboration does not make him the artwork’s author.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Playing Indian (1998); Indians in Unexpected Places (2004); Becoming Mary Sully: Toward an American Indian Abstract (2019). American Studies: A User’s Guide (2017) is coauthored with Alexander I. Olson and not reassigned as a sole work.
node.scope_note: New identity is Philip J. Deloria, the Harvard historian, not Vine Deloria Jr. or another relative. Publisher biography explicitly identifies Dakota descent; Indigenous-field context alone is not used to infer identity. Arguments use the bounded author Q&A; earlier monographs remain unread. Coauthors/editors and artwork ownership remain distinct. Later selected facts do not silently extend any group’s recorded review-through year.

incident_edges.relationship: Challenges a categorical boundary between Indigenous life and modernity through the case of Mary Sully’s art.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary written answer on being native to modernism, 2024. The argument concerns a distinctive artist and does not make her representative of all Indigenous people. The complete book remains unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Explains a collaborative route from family-held drawings through historical research and public talks to museum interpretation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary Q&A answers on rediscovery, curatorial challenges, book formation and exhibitions. Deloria credits his mother, audiences and named curators; this records historical/public interpretation, not sole creation of the art or a generic museum affiliation.

incident_edges.relationship: Deloria criticizes Turner’s frontier boundary for naturalizing Indigenous difference and an expectation of inevitable white triumph (2002).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher excerpt 8–10, with 6–7 framing. Deloria situates Turner within a longer frontier paradigm; this neither makes Turner its sole inventor nor treats all Indigenous historiography as one position. Remaining chapter unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Philip J. Deloria draws on Wilson’s account of oral tradition’s contextual rules and review by knowledgeable audiences when explaining its historical legitimacy (2002).
incident_edges.evidence_note: A specifically credited methodological resource in Deloria’s own chapter, not a claim of personal mentoring or a general career lineage. He cites Wilson’s 1997 essay, whose body remains unread here; the 1996 essay is a distinct work.

incident_edges.relationship: Deloria identifies a tension in Wilson’s oral-history argument between shared practices for checking accuracy and an epistemology that challenges Western historical knowledge (2002).
incident_edges.evidence_note: Qualified methodological reception within his recognition of Native historical authority. His characterization of purity and difference is attributed to him; it does not replace Wilson’s own situated family/community claims or her recorded acknowledgment of archival scholarship’s value and limits.

incident_edges.relationship: Deloria incorporates Dickason’s The Myth of the Savage into his account of critical scholarship on the images and discourses that accompanied conquest, crediting its extension to French contexts (2002).
incident_edges.evidence_note: A named historiographical resource, not personal mentoring or a comprehensive intellectual lineage. Deloria credits Gordon Sayre alongside Dickason. The particular paragraph on p.10 was freshly read and visually checked; Dickason’s book body remains unread. This claim is distinct from Deloria’s already mapped Turner criticism and Wilson resource.

named_group_routes.relationship: The middle ground: accommodation through mutual invention and creative misunderstanding between Algonquian villages and empires in the Great Lakes region, 1650–1815 (1991)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: White's own statement, The Middle Ground (1991). Introduction, p. ix (Cambridge Core first-page excerpt: the full page, folio observed): histories of Indian–white relations have had 'but two outcomes', stories 'of conquest and assimilation' or 'of cultural persistence'; their tellers 'miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys.' The next page (1991 p. x = 2011 p. xxvi; witnessed only by Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition, page images not seen, the 1991 page inferred) defines the middle ground, in paraphrase, as the space between cultures, between peoples, and between empires and the stateless world of villages, where differences were accommodated through creative and often expedient misunderstanding, and explains it by the long periods in which whites could neither command Indians nor ignore them. Chapter 2 opening (p. 50, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt, folio observed): French and Algonquians 'had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians.' It rested on 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners' (p. 52), and was, in paraphrase, a product both of everyday life and of formal diplomacy between distinct peoples (p. 53) (both Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 edition; page numbers as the snippet results give them, taken to match 1991). Chapter 3 opening (p. 94, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): the fur trade was 'a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange'. Epilogue (p. 518, Cambridge Core first-page excerpt): 'The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness.' In-period reception, each read in full. Savard (1992; Université de Montréal anthropologist) judges the book's circularity 'inattaquable' and suited to 'bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord', but asks whether the Algonquians' shattered prior state and Iroquois military supremacy, 'cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine', were needed to explain it (p. 120). Edmunds (1993) calls the thesis 'a valuable model for the exploration of the Indian-French relationship' (p. 148) and the book possibly 'a landmark volume in the ethnohistory of the Great Lakes tribes', but finds 'his arguments for the period after 1770 are less convincing' (p. 149). D. R. Miller (1994, Canadian Journal of Native Studies, from the Saskatchewan Indian Federated College) calls it 'an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations' (p. 157), notes that White 'deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian' (p. 158), and writes that 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious' (p. 170). The edge records a scholar's interpretation of Indigenous–imperial relations, which the Indigenous history entry lists as related scholarship; it does not make the work an Indigenous historical practice or a source of Indigenous authority. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: White's 2011 preface (Google Books search-within snippets only) answers Merrell's in-period critique (Into the American Woods, 1999; cited pp. xx–xxi) and the later critiques of Havard (Empire et métissages, 2003; p. xvi) and Deloria ('What Is the Middle Ground, Anyway?', 2006; cited p. xii; both unread here): the middle ground 'did not involve the achievement of a widespread mutual understanding and appreciation between Europeans and Indian peoples. People did not come together to love one another' (p. xxi), and he did not think that 'every time you find this process at work you would find the construction of a coherent space that is the equivalent of pays d'en haut' (p. xiii). McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF) reports that the concept 'struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37).

named_group_routes.relationship: Deloria criticized the culturally biased social-scientific approach of the workshops McNickle organized, as David Beck’s 1995 history reports.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Program-level criticism, not rejection of all McNickle’s writing. Beck identifies Deloria as a guest speaker at the 1965 workshop and one of its critics, citing Dorothy Parker (1992), p. 195; that book and Deloria’s original statement remain unread. Douglas Miller’s 2016 review separately describes a widening ideological gulf, while challenging a dismissive account of McNickle. Neither source establishes McNickle as Deloria’s mentor.

named_group_routes.relationship: Calloway identifies Deloria’s critique of outside experts as a continuing caution for his own practice and accountability to Native communities.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own interview section3 explicitly includes himself among non-Native researchers made to reconsider their methods. The1969 collection remains unread; this is acknowledged methodological use, not an inference about Indigenous identity.

named_group_routes.relationship: Native Studies does not belong under Ethnic Studies: to 'classify us as just another ethnic minority, it is colonialist'; 'we are not an ethnic minority … We are Indigenous', and 'Fourth World Studies is the next logical step' for comparison (1998; first given at UBC in 1995).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998): p. 33 (Native Studies 'does not belong under the rubric of Ethnic Studies'), p. 36 (Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins on lumping minority groups together), pp. 34–38 (Blauner's colonial model, whose conclusion she accepts while criticising his evidence), p. 40 ('colonialist'), p. 49 (conclusion). First presented at UBC, 2 November 1995 (p. 50 note). Protocol passages (pp. 38–39) are not used (OCAP).

named_group_routes.relationship: Wheeler opens her case that Indigenous peoples are not an ethnic minority with Deloria's Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) on liberals who 'categorize them all together' as minority groups, and returns to him on cooperative movements (1998).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Wicazo Sa Review 13:1 (1998), p. 36 (Deloria quoted, notes 6–9) and pp. 46–47 (Deloria 1969 on cooperative movements).

named_group_routes.relationship: Coulthard grounds his place-based critique in God Is Red: Deloria's 'distinction between Indigenous place-based and Western time-oriented understandings of the world' (2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 88 (read): Deloria's 'groundbreaking 1972 text, God is Red' holds that Western societies derive meaning 'in historical/developmental terms, thereby placing time as the narrative of central importance'; the quoted distinction is Coulthard's own wording; p. 89: land as a field of 'relationships of things to each other' (quoting Deloria 2001). The passage that follows, on Dene relations to land, is community knowledge and is not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. sources.title: Richard White, Introduction, The Middle Ground (1991), pp. ix–xvi, Cambridge University Press.

verification.note: Indexed primary introduction excerpt and print metadata checked. Cultural interaction is more complex than an absorption/resistance dichotomy. Regional scope is Great Lakes, 1650–1815. Online date 2012 is not the original publication date; full book and direct transmission to other scholars unchecked. Addendum 2026-10-13: Re-read for the 1.131 person entry. Chapter DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511584671.001 (Crossref: Introduction, pp. ix–xvi). The first-page excerpt, after an epigraph from James Clifford: 'The history of Indian-white relations has not usually produced complex stories. Indians are the rock, European peoples are the sea, and history seems a constant storm. There have been but two outcomes'; 'The first outcome produces stories of conquest and assimilation; the second produces stories of cultural persistence'; 'But the tellers of such stories miss a larger process and a larger truth. The meeting of sea and continent, like the meeting of whites and Indians, creates as well as destroys. Contact was not a battle of primal forces in which only one could survive. Something new could appear' (p. ix). The page continues in pe131_richard_white_middle_ground_1991 (p. x, via the 2011 edition).

sources.title: J. R. McNeill, “Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History,” History and Theory 42, no. 4 (December 2003): 5–43.
sources.citation: J. R. McNeill, “Observations on the Nature and Culture of Environmental History,” History and Theory 42:4 (2003): 5–43. doi:10.1046/j.1468-2303.2003.00255.x.

verification.note: Text-layer PDF of the article, read for pp. 8, 14–16 with notes 15, 34–35, 39, 42 (copy obtained on 2026-10-13; the route is not reused). Quoted: Hays 'Among the American pioneers in this field' (p. 8; n. 15 lists Conservation and the Gospel of Efficiency and Beauty, Health, and Permanence); 'the Annales historians were, many of them, strangely blind to evolving environments'; Braudel 'normally imagined it as an unchanging force'; Le Roy Ladurie 'embraced environmental change in two of his major books' (n. 35: Les paysans de Languedoc; Times of Feast, Times of Famine); 'To a very limited extent, then, Annales historians were engaged in environmental history avant la lettre'; 'Their general approach however proved inspirational' (all p. 14); n. 39 (p. 15): Nash 'in 1970 offered one of the very first courses in environmental history' (McNeill cites PHR '363 (1974)', a slip for 41, 1972); n. 42 (p. 16): 'The most important book in this vein probably was Roderick Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind'. Fix pass 2026-10-13 (sol-review-1.131): pp. 14 and 37–39 re-read. p. 14 as quoted above. p. 37: 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', and such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm nor attracted sizable schools of followers'; pp. 38–39: Merchant's scheme 'has not attracted wide imitation within environmental history'. [Also checked under pe131_crosby_mcneill_2003: later reading of the same copy; pp. 18–19, 24, 32–33 and 42 re-read for Crosby, page assignment from running heads. 'the American historians, especially Worster, Cronon, and Crosby, were read almost wherever environmental history aroused interest' (p. 19). The Columbian Exchange is 'one of the landmark works in environmental history' (p. 24). Ecological Imperialism is 'Perhaps the best-known among the thematically defined global-scale environmental histories' (p. 32) and 'contains one of the most elegant arguments found anywhere in environmental history'; 'Some readers felt that Crosby had relocated historical agency (and responsibility for genocide and colonialism) from humans to wheat and whooping cough' (p. 33). Crosby 'did not have much to say about the transplanting of agronomic practice' (p. 42).] [Also checked under pe131_richard_white_mcneill_2003: the White passage re-read: 'Richard White’s concept of “middle ground,” which he developed in the context of Native American–white relations in North America, struck historians of Japan and medieval Austria as useful for their own studies' (p. 37), n. 131 citing The Middle Ground and Brett Walker, The Conquest of Ainu Lands (2001).] Crossref 10.1046/j.1468-2303.2003.00255.x: History and Theory 42:4, 5–43. The linked publisher page (Wiley) is paywalled and did not supply the text read above. Addendum 2026-10-23: Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §3.1): Crossref record confirmed (History and Theory 42:4, pp. 5–43, issued 7 November 2003); the record's url now points to the publisher's DOI (batch source_field_sets); the pages read on 2026-10-13 stand on the earlier note, now without route identifiers. This wave checked metadata only.

sources.title: Richard White, The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1991).
sources.citation: Richard White, The Middle Ground: Indians, Empires, and Republics in the Great Lakes Region, 1650–1815 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1991), xvi, 544 p.

verification.note: Book-level record for the chapter openings and preview pages read for the 1.131 person entry; the introduction excerpt is ind127_white_1991. Crossref chapter records 10.1017/CBO9780511584671.001–.013 give the contents and 1991 pages: Introduction ix–xvi; 1 'Refugees: a world made of fragments' 1–49; 2 'The middle ground' 50–93; 3 'The fur trade' 94–141; 4 'The alliance' 142–185; 5 'Republicans and rebels' 186–222; 6 'The clash of empires' 223–268; 7 'Pontiac and the restoration of the middle ground' 269–314; 8 'The British alliance' 315–365; 9 'The contest of villagers' 366–412; 10 'Confederacies' 413–468; 11 'The politics of benevolence' 469–517; Epilogue 'Assimilation and otherness' 518–524. Cambridge Core first-page excerpts read for chapter 2 (p. 50: 'They had to arrive at some common conception of suitable ways of acting; they had to create what I have already referred to as a middle ground. The creation of the middle ground involved a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians'), chapter 3 (p. 94: 'The fur trade was a constantly changing compromise, a conduit, between two local models of the exchange - the French and the Algonquian') and the epilogue (p. 518: 'In different ways, both Anglo Americans and Algonquians subverted the middle ground in the nineteenth century. The compromises intrinsic in the middle ground yielded to stark choices between assimilation and otherness'). Google Books search-within snippets of the 2011 twentieth-anniversary edition (https://books.google.com/books?id=fHLfiOZVzmMC), whose body pagination matches 1991 (pp. 50, 53, 93, 518 carry the same text): p. xxvi (= 1991 p. x) 'The middle ground is the place in between: in between cultures, peoples, and in between empires and the nonstate world of villages'; 'It is the area between the historical foreground of European invasion and occupation and the background of Indian defeat and retreat. On the middle ground diverse peoples adjust their differences through what amounts to a process of creative, and often expedient, misunderstandings'; 'whites could neither dictate to Indians nor ignore them. Whites needed Indians as allies, as partners in exchange, as sexual partners, as friendly neighbors'; p. 52 'the need of people to find a means, other than force, to gain the cooperation or consent of foreigners'; p. 53 'It was both a product of everyday life and a product of formal diplomatic relations between distinct peoples'; p. 93 'rituals and ceremonials based on cultural parallels and congruences' (Edmunds 1993 prints 'congruencies'; D. R. Miller 1994 drops 'both' from the p. 53 sentence). Snippets only; the full text was not available (Internet Archive copies are lending-restricted). Fix pass 2026-10-13 (sol-review-1.131): a re-try to reach page images (Google Books page view) returned 403 on 2026-10-13, so the wording remains snippet-witnessed; atlas text paraphrases White's own framing passages and labels the rest as snippets.

sources.scope_note: In-period primary text: the middle-ground argument in White's words, at the checked pages only.

verification.note: Read in full (CJNS PDF, 10 pp., found through the University of Saskatchewan iPortal record 99). Author's address: Saskatchewan Indian Federated College, University of Regina. p. 157: 'The social and environmental historian Richard White has produced an extraordinary benchmark in the scholarship of European and Aboriginal relations in the Americas'; 'White demonstrates how the middle ground was a mutual creation of various Aboriginal North Americans and Europeans'. p. 158: 'he deemphasizes the specificity of a small number of groups in the larger Great Lakes region that are neither Iroquoian or Algonquian'. p. 169: White 'addresses the complexity of dependency and suggests that it “is an economic, political, and social relationship, but can also be an environmental relationship” (p.486)'; he 'examines formative influences ethnohistorically, with perspectives and theories drawn from political and economic anthropology, the historiographical insights of Braudel (longue duree) and others of the Annale School, and insights gleaned from the new cultural critique led by Edward Said'. p. 170: 'its impressive new standard for scholarship'; 'The challenge for a similar study with emphasis upon the north side of the Great Lakes is obvious'. Page numbers from the running heads.

sources.scope_note: In-period Canadian review essay: the middle ground as benchmark, its environmental dimension and its limits.

sources.title: Rémi Savard, review of Richard White, The Middle Ground (1991), Journal de la Société des Américanistes 78, no. 1 (1992): 119–120.
sources.citation: Rémi Savard, review of White, The Middle Ground, Journal de la Société des Américanistes 78:1 (1992): 119–120.

verification.note: Read in full in the Persée page text (pp. 119–120); signed '[Rémi Savard, Département d'Anthropologie, Université de Montréal]' (Persée indexes him as Rémy). p. 119: the story begins where Trigger's Children of Aataentsic (1976) ends; Savard translates pp. 1–2 ('ils reconstituèrent un monde nouveau au moyen des débris de l'ancien'); White's thesis is that French and Algonquians needed each other against the Iroquois, producing what he 'nomme un Middle Ground'. p. 120: he translates p. xv ('Les Américains ont inventé les Indiens et les ont forcés à vivre avec les conséquences de cette image tardive'); the book 'donne le meilleur de lui-même lorsqu'il décrit les relations concrètes entre les gens dans les villages multi-ethniques du Middle Ground'; 'La circularité qu'il met en relief me paraît inattaquable. Je crois même qu'elle convient pour bien d'autres époques et régions de l'Amérique du Nord'; but it may not have been necessary 'd'invoquer la dévastation iroquoise et la nécessité d'un arbitre européen', and 'on peut se demander si l'état antérieur de ces Algonquiens ne provient pas de notre imagination, tout comme l'état de débandade présumée après 1450 ne tient pas à cette suprématie militaire iroquoise, cet autre mythe fondateur de la république américaine'. The Persée PDF is behind an altcha check; the page-text layer was read.

sources.scope_note: In-period review by a Quebec anthropologist: praise for the circular argument and doubt about its premise.

The body of Wilson’s cited 1997 essay remains unread. The older Turner claim and its qualifications remain intact.
